tagline.text: A triangular 1796 Spanish coastal watchtower with Bohol Strait views

location.label: Location
location.text: Punta Cruz, Maribojoc, Bohol, on the headland at Maribojoc's western tip

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (can be part of a Bohol day tour)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0~500 (small or no entrance fee; round-trip transport from Tagbilaran included as an estimate)

children.text: The Punta Cruz Watchtower is a Spanish coastal watchtower completed in 1796 on the headland at the western tip of Maribojoc, Bohol. It was built to guard against Moro raiders, is described as the only watchtower in the Philippines with an isosceles-triangle floor plan, and is designated a National Historical Landmark and National Cultural Treasure. Restored after the 2013 earthquake, it offers views over the Bohol Strait from its second-floor windows.

The Punta Cruz Watchtower is a small stone fort standing on a headland that juts into the sea at the western end of Maribojoc, on Bohol's northwest coast. Its formal name is the Fort of Saint Vincent Ferrer (Fuerte de San Vicente Ferrer), and it is dedicated to Saint Vincent Ferrer, Maribojoc's second patron saint. According to Wikipedia, it was completed in 1796 under the supervision of the Augustinian Recollect priest Manuel Sanchez de Nuestra Sra. del Tremendal, as one of a network of defenses against fleets of Moro slave raiders coming from the south.

The tower's most striking feature is its shape. The base is an isosceles triangle that connects on the second level to a short hexagonal tower, and it is described as the only watchtower in the Philippines with a triangular floor plan. It is built of neatly cut coral stone and wood. Above the entrance there is an inscription with the Spanish coat of arms and the construction date, and the central room keeps a niche for an image of Saint Vincent Ferrer. Some of the wooden beams that support the masonry walls also survive, giving a glimpse of the building methods of the time.

The tower was declared a National Historical Landmark in February 2009, and on August 29, 2011 it was designated a National Cultural Treasure together with the other Bohol watchtowers. Since 2006 it has also been on UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the Spanish Colonial Fortifications of the Philippines. The magnitude 7.2 earthquake of October 15, 2013 caused moderate to serious damage, and restoration work continued from 2016. A 2023 media report says it was restored to its original state. On the headland there is also a wooden cross standing in a cleft in the rock. According to local tradition the cross glowed to warn the town when raiders approached, and the name Punta Cruz is said to come from punta (point of land) and cruz (cross). From the top of the tower you can see Cebu Island across the Bohol Strait, and locals also enjoy it as a picnic spot.

Around Maribojoc there are several traces of the late 18th century, when Moro raiders often targeted coastal towns. Bohol's coast still has several similar watchtowers, and Punta Cruz is one of the Bohol watchtowers jointly designated as National Cultural Treasures. It is a defensive structure no longer in use, but if you stand inside the stone walls and look out the seaward windows you can faintly picture residents scanning the horizon for ships. Entrance fees and opening hours in this guide differ between official sources and blogs, so I have marked them "check locally"; please confirm once more before you visit.

The base is an isosceles triangle that narrows into a hexagonal tower as it rises, which is an unusual structure. One guide says the apex points toward the sea. It is described as the only triangular-plan watchtower in the Philippines, so photograph it from both the front and the side.
You can still see walls of cut coral stone and, above the entrance, the Spanish royal coat of arms and an inscription of the construction date.

blocks.title: Bohol Strait from the second-floor windows

children.text: The second level, reached by a staircase, has wide openings in the walls from which you can see the Bohol Strait and Cebu Island on the far side. Climbing in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower, is more comfortable. Because the openings are wide, do not lean out near the edges.
An image of Saint Vincent Ferrer is kept in the niche of the central room. It shows that the tower was both a defensive structure and a place of the town's faith.
A wooden cross stands in a cleft of rock beside the tower. Tradition says it glowed to warn of approaching raiders, and it is said to be the origin of the name Punta Cruz.

It became a National Historical Landmark in 2009 and a National Cultural Treasure in 2011, and was restored after the 2013 earthquake. Knowing its restoration history, you can have fun spotting the difference between new and old stone.
The area around the headland is also used by local families who bring a packed meal to relax. Stalls selling simple food, water and souvenirs are said to be there.
Board a Maribojoc-bound jeepney or bus at the Tagbilaran terminal. Guides say it takes about
40–50 minutes
to reach Maribojoc.
Get off in Maribojoc town and look around the church and the area in front of the town hall.
Continue to the junction for Punta Cruz. For the last stretch, walk or take a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal).

Look around the tower and the cross, then climb the stairs to enjoy the strait view from the second floor. Guides mention limits on the number of people inside and on how long you can stay, so follow the on-site instructions.
Have a snack at a nearby stall and return the same way.
Punta Cruz is often included on Bohol day tours. Maribojoc is about
22km

northwest of Tagbilaran. Because it is a restored tower, the interior is small and it is hard for many people to climb at once. If you avoid times that overlap with tour groups you can see it at leisure, and checking the return jeepney times in advance gives peace of mind.
Leave Tagbilaran for Maribojoc in a rental car or tour vehicle.
Stop at the Punta Cruz Watchtower to take photos and enjoy the view.
Have lunch and see heritage sites such as the church in Maribojoc town.
Take an Abatan River firefly tour around dusk or head back to Tagbilaran.

From Maribojoc town to the Punta Cruz junction is about
2km
, and you cover the last stretch by motorcycle taxi or on foot.
Guides say private vehicles can drive close to the tower. By public transport you may have to walk from the junction.
It is often included on Bohol heritage tours that depart from Panglao or Tagbilaran. The usual route also covers Baclayon Church, the Loboc River and the Chocolate Hills.

If you rent a vehicle, linking Punta Cruz with Maribojoc Church or an Abatan River tour makes the day far more efficient. Prices for a car with a driver vary widely by company, so get a quote before you set off.
Punta Cruz is an outdoor monument, so the dry season with less rain is the most comfortable. There is almost no shade at midday, so early morning or late afternoon is best.
In the rainy season the coastal path can be slippery and waves high, so be careful near the headland.

During the day, photos come out best in the early morning and late afternoon when the sun is low. Since the tower is described as facing northeast, the light at midday is flat and brings out less of the stone texture. Plan a sunset visit only if you have your own vehicle, because public transport back may stop running.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The best views and the most comfortable season for a picnic.
The sun is strong, so go in the early morning or around sunset.
The stairs and headland are wet and slippery; do not go during a typhoon.

Maribojoc has small resorts and riverside lodgings, and around the Abatan River some places rent floating cottages. Many travelers stay in Panglao or Tagbilaran and fit Punta Cruz into a day plan.

Near the headland there are said to be stalls selling simple food, drinks and souvenirs. For a proper meal, you will have more choice in Maribojoc town or back in Tagbilaran. It is safest to bring water and snacks.
Before you reach Punta Cruz, withdraw cash and buy water. If you go around lunchtime, the hours of the stalls near the headland may not be regular, so you might bring a simple packed lunch.
Guides mention a limit of 50 people inside at once and a stay of about 45 minutes, so an early hour is easier than mid-morning when tourists crowd in.

Entrance fees and opening hours differ between guides, so confirm with the on-site staff when you arrive. One source gives 8:00–17:00 but it is not confirmed, and an older Bohol tourism listing mentions Fridays and weekends, so check more carefully if you visit on a weekday.
The last stretch may be on foot, so wear comfortable shoes.
The cross and rocks on the headland can be wet and slippery from the waves.
There is almost no shade, so a hat, sunscreen and water are essential.
If you add it to a Bohol heritage day, plan the order of stops toward Baclayon Church and the Loboc River in advance.
Do not write on the interior walls or take away any stones.
This is a restored monument, so watch your footing while taking photos where there is no railing.
Deciding on three shots in advance, the front entrance, the cross on the headland and the strait from the second-floor window, makes a full record even in a short visit.
Other heritage sites in Maribojoc and the firefly tour each take time, so rather than fitting them all into one day, narrow it to two stops.
The number of people inside and the length of stay may be limited, and the stairs and headland are slippery, so follow on-site instructions.
Entrance fees and opening hours differ by source, so always confirm locally.
Do not go out onto the headland on typhoon days or when waves are high.
It is a monument restored after the 2013 earthquake damage, so do not lean on or climb the structure.
Public transport is not frequent, so check the return times beforehand.
Agree on the motorcycle taxi fare before you set off.
While absorbed in photography, do not move toward the edge of the headland or the rock crevices. Waves can rise suddenly.
